sections.h2: Which statute applies to a rented house?
sections.html:
It turns on the size and use of the building. N.J.S.A. 2A:18-53 governs commercial space, residential buildings with at most two rental units, and a three-family house where the owner lives in one unit. Nearly every other residential rental falls under N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 and the sections after it, known as the Anti-Eviction Act. Hotels, motels and seasonal rentals sit outside it.

Landlord-tenant lawsuits start in the Special Civil Part of Superior Court, at the courthouse serving the rental's county. Corporations, LLCs and limited partnerships must be represented by a New Jersey attorney. Sole owners and general partners may speak for themselves. Before you put a tenant-occupied house on the market, decide which of the two statutes covers it, since that sets the notice periods below.

sections.h2: Does selling the house let the owner remove a tenant?
sections.html:
Not by itself. Under the Anti-Eviction Act a covered tenant can be removed only for a cause the statute lists, and signing a sale contract with an investor is not on that list. The buyer simply becomes landlord under the existing lease.

Two sale-linked grounds do exist. An owner of a building with three residential units or fewer may recover a unit after contracting to sell it to a buyer who intends to live there, if the contract requires the unit to be empty at closing. For condominium and cooperative units, a similar ground reaches tenants whose tenancy began after the master deed was recorded, but only when the tenant received the disclosure statement required by N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.9. The remaining grounds include:

  • nonpayment of rent, or chronic late payment after a written warning
  • disorderly behavior or intentional damage to the premises
  • continued violation of reasonable house rules or lease terms after a written warning
  • refusal of reasonable lease changes when a term ends
  • permanent retirement of the building from residential use
  • conversion to condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership

A seller whose buyer wants vacant possession needs either the small-building own-use ground or the tenant's cooperation.

sections.h2: Written notice before an eviction suit
sections.html:
Lead time ranges from three days to three years, depending on the ground. N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2 requires a written demand that describes the cause in detail. It can be handed to the tenant, left with a household member over 14 at the tenant's home, or mailed by certified mail, with a regular-mail copy if the certified letter is not picked up. Plain nonpayment cases are exempt from this requirement.

Lead time under N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2
GroundNotice period
Disorderly conduct, damage to the unit, or certain drug-offense grounds3 days
House-rule or lease violations, habitual late rent, refused lease changes1 month
Owner must board up, demolish or correct cited violations3 months

Conversion to condominium or cooperative3 years, and no suit before the lease expires

sections.h2: Who holds the security deposit after a sale?
sections.html:
The buyer ends up holding it, and the seller has to move it. N.J.S.A. 46:8-20 directs an owner who conveys a rental to pass the deposit and the tenant's accrued interest to the grantee when the deed is delivered or within five days afterward. The seller then tells the tenant by registered or certified mail who the new holder is and where to reach them. The buyer has a duty of its own to demand those funds from the seller.

Once the money is turned over, N.J.S.A. 46:8-21 frees the seller from liability to the tenant. The buyer stays answerable for proper investment, notices, interest and the eventual refund, whether or not the seller ever sent the funds. Other Security Deposit Law rules your file should reflect:

  • the deposit is capped at one and a half months of rent, and yearly increases are limited to 10 percent of the existing deposit
  • the tenant gets written notice of the bank, account type, rate and amount, repeated after any change of ownership
  • no deductions are allowed while the tenant still lives in the unit
  • the refund, with itemized charges, is due a month after the lease ends
  • a tenant who proves wrongful withholding recovers double plus costs, and claims up to $5,000 go to small claims

An owner-occupied building with two or fewer rental units is outside the law unless the tenant gives 30 days' written notice invoking it.

sections.h2: The court process step by step
sections.html:
Removal takes a judge and a court officer, and a landlord who bypasses either has locked the tenant out illegally. The landlord files a verified complaint with a case information statement, the lease and a registration statement. Court charges are $50 for one tenant and $5 for each additional one, plus a $7 service charge. The first trial date falls at least 21 days after the summons is served.

Tenants must come to court, because written answers are not accepted. A missing landlord means dismissal, and a missing tenant means default. If both show up, court staff first offer a settlement conference, and the judge hears the case only if that fails. A win for the landlord produces a judgment for possession, which leads to these steps:

  • a three-business-day wait before the landlord may ask for a warrant of removal, which costs $35 plus mileage
  • service of the warrant by a court officer, who allows a residential tenant three business days to leave
  • a 30-day window to apply for the warrant after judgment, unless a court order or signed agreement pauses it

In rent cases, a tenant who pays everything owed plus lawful costs stops the process, even up to three business days after being removed, and a landlord who refuses risks a $500 penalty. Tenants may also seek up to seven days of orderly removal, or a hardship stay of up to six months with all rent paid.

sections.h2: Defenses that can slow the sale of a tenant-occupied home
sections.html:
A buyer will ask about these before closing. Under the Marini Doctrine of habitability, a tenant who pays the rent into court may argue that heat, hot water, a working toilet or safe stairways were missing. That argument cannot excuse repeated late payment or lease violations.

Registration is another checkpoint. A small owner-occupied building registers with the Community Development Authority, and every other rental registers with the Bureau of Housing Inspection. The statement goes in with the complaint. Tenants can also argue the tenancy is illegal, for example an unapproved extra apartment, or ask for a rent abatement. When a public agency subsidizes the rent, the landlord must notify that agency and attach proof.

A foreclosure does not wipe out a lease. A tenant in good standing is not forced to move, and whoever buys at the sheriff's sale takes the building subject to the tenant's rights.

Gather what a title agent and buyer will ask for. Call the Special Civil Part office serving the property for its current fee schedule, since court charges change, and ask the municipal clerk whether a local rental license applies.

  • every signed lease and renewal, with a rent roll
  • deposit notices and the bank statement showing where each deposit sits
  • the rental registration statement
  • any notice to cease, notice to quit or court filing
  • repair requests and invoices

An owner who needs the house empty has two honest options: wait for the lease to run out and negotiate a move-out date, or sell to a buyer who takes the tenancy as is. A cash buyer who accepts the house with the tenant in place avoids the repair and financing steps, though the lease and deposit still pass to that buyer.

faqs.q: Can a New Jersey landlord shut off utilities to push a tenant out?
faqs.a: No. Changing locks, padlocking doors or cutting gas, water or electricity is illegal. A tenant locked out this way can file in the Special Civil Part and ask to be let back in, along with money damages.

faqs.q: What happens to a lease when the owner sells?
faqs.a: The lease generally carries on. A buyer steps into the landlord's position, and the only sale-based exception is a buyer who will personally live in a unit of a building with three or fewer units and wants it empty at closing.

faqs.q: How soon must a deposit be refunded?
faqs.a: Within 30 days after the lease ends, delivered in person or by registered or certified mail, with the tenant's share of interest and an itemized list of any deductions. Wrongful withholding can cost the landlord double the amount.

faqs.q: Can a tenant keep the home after a judgment for possession?
faqs.a: Sometimes. In a nonpayment case, paying all rent and costs within three business days of the judgment or the eviction ends it. A hardship stay can last up to six months, and orderly removal up to seven days.

faqs.q: Does an LLC landlord need a lawyer in landlord-tenant court?
faqs.a: Yes. Corporations, LLCs and limited partnerships must be represented by a New Jersey attorney, while sole proprietors and general partners may represent themselves.
